Following discussion w/ Bruno on 19/06/26

### Analysis :

- 1 Ne/NT as categorical variable
  - a Linear discriminant analysis
  - b Analysis non supervised (PCA) & projection
  - c Multinomial linear model (not done here because too many variables for nb of points)
- 2 Ne/NT as quantitative variable (slope with Fmax)

### Specificity :

If using variables outputs from OSMOSE :

- Think about removing the points where abundance is too low
- Need to standardise the variables :
  - e.g. collect data of birth rate, only for cohort of age i, with i = 100% mature individuals in the cohort (abundance tot age a cohort c = abundance mat age a cohort c)
  - e.g. collect data of mortality rate : use the cumulated mortality rate between ages of cohort c
- Last step : average betweeen Fmax and replicates

### Variables selected :

coherently with my previous work about the relationship between maintenance rate and LHT (life history traits)

| THV | OSMOSE parameter or output variable |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| TL | ratio.min, ratio.max |
| a_mat/L_mat | m0, m1 |
| a_max | lifespan |
| fecundity | egg.weight, maturity.r |
| Growth coefficient | predation.ingestion, Topt, c_m |
| Mortality | variables : starvation, predation, foraging, additional mortality rate |
|  | parameter : mortality.additional.larva.rate |
| Selectivity | centered |

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = T}

df_Topt <- read.csv(paste0(here::here(), "/DATA/FromOSMOSE-nsConfiguration_outputs_global_complet.csv"))[, c("Species", "Final_Topt")]
# names   <- rfishbase::species(stringr::str_replace(df_Topt$Species, "_", " "))

# match up scientific names to species names in OSMOSE
names <- read.csv(file=paste0(here::here(), "/DATA/names_species_rfishbase.csv"))
names_commun <- names[, c("Species", "FBname")]
colnames(df_Topt)[which(colnames(df_Topt)=="Species")] <- "Spe_scien"
colnames(names_commun)[which(colnames(names_commun)=="Species")] <- "Spe_scien"
colnames(names_commun)[which(colnames(names_commun)=="FBname")] <- "Species"
names_commun$Spe_scien <- stringr::str_replace(names_commun$Spe_scien, " ", "_")
tempo <- stringr::str_split(names_commun$Species, " ")
tempo <- sapply(1:length(tempo), function(x) {
  if (length(tempo[[x]])==1) return(tempo[[x]])
  if (length(tempo[[x]])==3) tempo[[x]] <- c(paste0(toupper(substr(tempo[[x]][2], 1, 1)), substr(tempo[[x]][2], 2, nchar(tempo[[x]][2]))), tempo[[x]][3])
  new_name <- paste0(tempo[[x]][1], toupper(substr(tempo[[x]][2], 1, 1)), substr(tempo[[x]][2], 2, nchar(tempo[[x]][2])))
  if(new_name == c("EuropeanHake")) new_name <- "Hake"
  return(new_name)
})
names_commun$Species <- tempo
names_commun$Species <- stringr::str_replace(names_commun$Species, " ", "")
df_Topt <- full_join(df_Topt, names_commun)
df_Topt[which(df_Topt$Spe_scien %in% c("Ammodytes_spp", "Crangon_crangon")), "Species"] <- c("Sandeel", "Shrimp")
```

2- Prepare dataset with the configuration parameters

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = T}
# extract ony the parameters I need
nspecies <- osmose::get_par(conf, "simulation.nspecies") -1 #because we removed the Shrimp
df_param <-as.data.frame(sapply(c("ratio.max", "ratio.min",
                            "m0", "m1",
                            "lifespan",                             
                            "egg.weight", "maturity.r",
                            "predation.ingestion",
                            "maint.energy.c_m",                             
                            "mortality.additional.larva.rate",  
                            #"mortality.additional.rate", 
                            "species.name"
  ), 
  FUN = function(x) {
    a <- osmose::get_par(conf, x)    
    if (length(a)>nspecies) a <- a[c(1:nspecies)]
    b <- names(a)
    a <- sapply(1:length(a), FUN=function(x) a [[x]] <- a[[x]][length(a[[x]])])
    names(a) <- b
    a <- unlist(a)
}))
df_param$spi <- unlist(stringr::str_split(rownames(df_param), "max."))[seq(2, 2*nrow(df_param), by=2)]
colnames(df_param)[which(colnames(df_param) == "species.name")] <- "Species"

```

4- Prepare dataset of the selectivity curve

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = T}
path_csv <- "C:/Users/mbeneat/Documents/osmose/Chap2/osmose-ns/osmose-ns-v4.4.1_clim/fishing_rate"
df_select <- as.data.frame(matrix(-99, ncol=2, nrow=length(list.files(path_csv, pattern = "csv", full.names = T))))
colnames(df_select) <- c("selectq90", "spi")
k=0
for (csv in list.files(path_csv, pattern = "csv", full.names = T)){
  k=k+1
  f <- read.csv(csv)
  f_1 <- f[1, -1]
  f_1 <- f_1[-which(f_1 == 0)]
  q90 <- as.numeric(quantile(as.numeric(f_1), probs = 0.9))
  df_select$selectq90[k] = as.numeric(f_1[which(as.numeric(f_1)>=(q90))[1]])
  df_select$spi[k] <- stringr::str_remove(unlist(stringr::str_split(csv, pattern = "file."))[2], pattern = ".csv")
}
```

## ANALYSIS

### Linear discriminant analysis - LDA

<!-- <https://www.sthda.com/english/articles/36-classification-methods-essentials/146-discriminant-analysis-essentials-in-r/>  -->

The LDA algorithm starts by finding directions that maximize the separation between classes, then use these directions to predict the class of individuals. These directions, called linear discriminants, are a linear combinations of predictor variables. LDA assumes that predictors are normally distributed (Gaussian distribution) and that the different classes have class-specific means and equal variance/covariance. Before performing LDA, consider: - Inspecting the univariate distributions of each variable and make sure that they are normally distribute. - If not, you can transform them using log and root for exponential distributions and Box-Cox for skewed distributions. - removing outliers from your data and standardize the variables to make their scale comparable. The linear discriminant analysis can be easily computed using the function lda() [MASS package].

1- Density diagram

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = T}
ggplotdata <- train.data[which(sapply(train.data, is.numeric))]
ggplotdata$id <- 1:nrow(ggplotdata) 
ggplotdata <- pivot_longer(ggplotdata, cols=-c("id"), values_to = "density", names_to = "variable") 
ggplot(ggplotdata)+ 
  geom_density(aes(density))+ 
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales="free")
ggplot(ggplotdata, aes(sample=density))+ 
  stat_qq()+ 
  stat_qq_line()+ 
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales="free")
```


3- Fit the model : 3 categories of responses of Ne/N to ↑ Fishing mortality rate

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = T}
model1 <- lda(`Ne/N_1` ~., data = train.transformed[, -which(colnames(train.transformed) == "Ne/N_2")]) 
predictions <- model1 %>% predict(test.transformed[, -which(colnames(train.transformed) == "Ne/N_2")]) 
head(predictions$class, 6)
head(predictions$posterior, 6) 
head(predictions$x, 3)
names(predictions)
```

4- Plot model

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = T}
lda.data <- cbind(train.transformed, predict(model1)$x) 
# ggplot(lda.data, aes(LD1, LD2, label=rownames(lda.data))) + 
#   geom_point(aes(color = `Ne/N_1`), size=2)+ 
#   geom_text(hjust=0, vjust=0) #Model accuracy 
mean(predictions$class==test.transformed$`Ne/N_1`) #0 = bad, 1=Good

axis_expl <- model1$scaling #a matrix which transforms observations to discriminant functions, normalized so that within groups covariance matrix is spherical. 
pi1 <- ggplot(lda.data, aes(`LD1`, `LD2`)) + 
  geom_jitter(aes(color = `Ne/N_1`), size=2)+ 
  geom_text_repel(hjust=0, vjust=0, max.overlaps = 15, aes(label=rownames(lda.data)))+ 
  geom_segment(data=axis_expl, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = (LD1/0.5), yend = (LD2/0.5)), arrow = arrow(length = unit(1/2, "picas")), color="grey51") + 
  geom_text_repel(data=axis_expl, aes(x = (LD1/0.5), y = (LD2/0.5), label=rownames(axis_expl)), color="grey51", max.overlaps = 100)+ 
  labs(title="LDA analysis explaining the species' Ne/N variation with their traits") 
ggsave(pi1, file=paste0(here::here(), "/output/PLOTS/LDA1.pdf"))

```

5- PLOTS

[FIGURE]{.underline} : LDA with 5 categories of responses of Ne/N to ↑ Fishing mortality rate:

Here we have 5 categories of Ne/N. The discriminant analysis worked well and all five categories are well differentiated. We expected the 'decreasing' (blue) and 'constantVkincreasing' (green) categories to be related, as well as the 'increasing' (pink) and 'constantVkdecreasing' (yellow). The 'constant' category is separated, and that was also expected.

All the traits participate equally in describing the distribution of Ne/N, except for maintenance.c_m and maturity.r. Species with longest lifespan, largest larval mortality, highest minimum predation ratio and lowest egg weight and optimal temperature tend to have an increasing Ne/N. Species with a constant Ne/NT are the ones with the highest predation ingestion, max predation ratio, shortest lifespan, largest egg weight, fastest maturation and lowest selectivity size. Lastly, species with average parameter values tend to have a decreasing Ne/N.

We can relate the resilience level of the species to exploitation, to the pace of life syndrome theory : species with the fastest pace of life are the least affected by fishing mortality (red) : they are characterized by short lifespan and large egg weight. Species with the slowest pace of life (yellow, pink) (late maturation, longer lifespan, lowest optimal temperature) are the ones the most resilient to exploitation : increasing Ne/N. Lastly, the species the least resilient to exploitation are the ones with intermediate (blue, green) life-history strategies.

Weird :

- species with the slow pace of life have the highest larval mortality ? - maintenance.c_m and maturity.r not explaining the variance in Ne/NT ?
- slow paced of life species have the largest egg.weight ? certainly related to the way it is calculated =\> osmose egg.weight = maturity.r/fecundity

```{r}
Z <- predict(model1)$x
# Coefficients des variables
A <- model1$scaling
# Reconstruction approximative
Xhat <- Z %*% t(A)
Xhat
```

[FIGURE]{.underline} : LDA with 3 categories of responses of Ne/N to ↑ Fishing mortality rate:

Here we have 3 categories of Ne/N. The discriminant analysis worked well and all three categories are well differentiated.

The traits participating in describing the variance of Ne/N have an heterogeneous size effect. The predatory behavior differentiates the species with increasing against constant Ne/N. Top predators have rather a constant Ne/N, while species with fast maturation, high mortalities and shortest lifespan have an increasing Ne/N. Lastly, intermediate species in terms of predation behaviour are differentiated by the lowest maturation slope, shortest lifespan, highest egg weight, lowest maturity.r, highest predation.ingestion, highest Madd and lowest larval mortality rate and highest selectivity highest Topt.

Weird : - inconsistent with first lda plot, I believe it is due to the subcategories that bring nuance that is not included here. I trust more the 5 categories LDA than the 3 categories LDA.

The PCA, using PCA2 and PCA3, to differentiate the 3 groups of responses of Ne/N to increasing exploitation isolates the 'decreasing' category. These species are chatecterised by low ratio.min and average larval mortality. The other traits do not participate to explain the categories of Ne/N. Plus, the percentage of variance explained is null.

```{r}
fviz_pca_biplot(res.pca, axes = c(2,3), col.ind = df$`Ne/N_1`)
```

The PCA, using PCA2 and PCA3, to differentiate the 5 groups of responses of Ne/N to increasing exploitation isolates the 'decreasing', 'constantVkincreasing' and 'constant' categories. 'decreasing' and 'constantVkincreasing' species are characterised by low ratio.min and average larval mortality. The 'constant' category species are chatacterised by low ratio.min and larval mortality. Plus, the percentage of variance explained is null.

### Ne/NT as quantitative variable (slope with Fmax)

1- Estimate the slope of Ne/N with Fmax

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = T}
Ne_NT = NULL 
for (sp in rownames(df)){ #load and filter data 
  load(file=paste0(pathoutputRDATA, "/Complete_INIT2", sp, ".RData")) 
  final_dataset_age = complete[[2]] 
  rm(complete)
  NeNT <- final_dataset_age[which(final_dataset_age$variable %in% c("Ne_N_alpha", "NT")), -which(colnames(final_dataset_age) %in% c("age", "Fstart"))] 
  rm(final_dataset_age) 
  if (is.null(Ne_NT)) {Ne_NT <- pivot_wider(NeNT, values_from = "value", names_from = "variable") 
  } else Ne_NT <- rbind(Ne_NT, pivot_wider(NeNT, values_from = "value", names_from = "variable")) 
}
Ne_NT       <- Ne_NT[-which(Ne_NT$NT < 10), ] # removing the cases of low abundance( = collapses )
Ne_NT$Ne_NT <- Ne_NT$Ne_N_alpha/Ne_NT$NT 
Ne_NT       <- Ne_NT[, -which(colnames(Ne_NT) %in% c("Ne_N_alpha", "NT"))]

Ne_NT <- Ne_NT %>% 
  group_by(Species, replicate) %>% 
  nest() %>% 
  mutate(model = map(data, ~lm(Ne_NT ~ 1 + Fmax, data = .x) %>% tidy)) %>% 
  unnest(model) %>% 
  filter(term == 'Fmax') %>% ungroup() 
Ne_NT <- Ne_NT[, c("Species", "estimate", "replicate")] 
Ne_NT <- Ne_NT %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarise(Ne_NT = mean(estimate, na.rm = T)) %>% 
  ungroup()

```

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = T}
df_sp$Species <- rownames(df) 
df_Ne_NT2 <- full_join(df_sp, Ne_NT, by = "Species") 
df_Ne_NT2 <- df_Ne_NT2[, -which(colnames(df_Ne_NT2) %in% c("Species", "Ne/N_2", "Ne/N_1"))]

lm(data = df_Ne_NT, formula = Ne_NT ~ PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5 + PC6 + PC7 + PC8 + PC9 + PC10 + PC11 + PC12 + PC13)

fit <- plsr(Ne_NT ~ ., data = df_Ne_NT2, scale = TRUE, validation = "CV")
```

3- RESULTS

[What is the estimated effect of each variable on y?]{.underline}

```{r}
coef(fit, ncomp = 5)
```

Here, we can relate the slope of the curve Ne/N \~ Fmax (positive, negative) to the variables changes. What is emerging is that : species with slow pace of life (high ratio.min, late maturation, low egg weight, low predation ingestion, and high c_m (? this is not coherent with my 1st chapter) or larval mortality) have Positive Ne/N \~ Fmax. On the contrary, species with the decreasing slopes are characterized by short lifespan and low egg weight, thus a fast pace of life.

[How important was the variable in building the predictive components?]{.underline} Variables with Variable Importance in Projection indec (VIP) \> 1 are usually considered important:

```{r}
VIP(fit, opt.comp = 5)
```

This result indicates which variables are the most influential on Ne/N. Two main dimensions emerge : (1) the fast-slow dimensions represented by the maturation speed (m0, m1), the preferred habitat temperature range (Topt) and the egg weight which have a VIP variable \>1, (2) the predation behavior which is represented by the predation size ranges preferred by the predator (ratio.min) and the maximum predation ingestion rate (predation.ingestion).
